E0737.summary: An expression, in a quoted adept's voice, for the agent and patient of the work, which must be united in friendship and love.
E0737.body: Voiced by the Adept Atwood quotes: the Heaven and Earth philosophical are treated as agent and patient, “the Heaven and Earth philosophical, even as agent and patient” [IV.2 ¶30], which must be united in friendship and love. Asserted identity: = agent and patient [IV.2 ¶30].

E0738.summary: The Benedictine Monk's own fire, which stirs up the elemental fire; set against coals and common fire.
E0738.body: In the words of the Benedictine Monk (quoted): “For I have my heavenly fire, which excites and stirs up the elemental one” [III.3 ¶24]. This fire excites the elemental fire as the matter desires a fitting Form, and is contrasted with coals and common fire [III.3 ¶24].

E0739.summary: With 'the fire', one of the two agents of the work, glossed by the scholiast as the external and internal agents of the Hermetic work.
E0739.body: A quoted scholiast reads the pair: “By the fire and heavenly bird are dignified, says the scholiast, the external and internal agents in the Hermetic work” [I.3 n16]. The heavenly Flyer (or bird) is thus paired with the fire as one of these agents; the text does not say which of the two is external and which internal.

E0740.summary: The Hebrew teaching, which Atwood says differs from the Ethnic Anima Mundi only in words.
E0740.body: Atwood compares the Hebrew doctrine with the Ethnic Anima Mundi and finds that it differs from it only in words [I.2 ¶14].

E0741.summary: Hebrew Kabalists and Rabbis, cited by Atwood in support of absolute Idealism, the fall and reunion of creation, reason over authority, and self-inquiry.
E0741.body: Atwood cites the Hebrew Kabalists and Rabbis in support of absolute Idealism, of creation's fall and reunion, of reason over authority, and of self-inquiry [II.1 ¶40; II.1 ¶41].

E0742.summary: A group voice whose 'precious death' Atwood equates with the gate of blackness.
E0742.body: Atwood equates the “precious death” of the Hebrews and Academics with the gate of blackness [II.3 ¶37].

E0743.summary: A modern metaphysician whose doctrine of pure Being Atwood contrasts with the Hermetic way, and whom the Appendix lists among moderns who drew on the Mystics.
E0743.body: Atwood quotes “the German philosopher (Hegel)”: “All things, says the German philosopher (Hegel), have their commencement in pure Being” [III.2 ¶30]. She uses this as a contrast: abstraction reaches pure Being, which is equal to non-Being, but only as a void [III.2 ¶30]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) he is named among modern metaphysicians who took their starting point from the Mystics [APP ¶96], and appears again in the same list as one who 'saw it' [APP ¶117].

E0744.summary: Author to whom the mystical romance Theagenes and Chariclea is attributed; named among writers of extant treatises on the philosophers' stone.
E0744.body: The mystical romance *Theagenes and Chariclea* is attributed to Heliodorus, who, the book says, resigned his bishopric of Tricca rather than disavow it [I.1 ¶28; I.1 n34]. He is also named with Olympiodorus, Synesius, Athenagoras, Zosimus and Archelaus as an author of extant treatises on the philosophers’ stone [I.1 ¶27; I.1 n34].

E0745.summary: 'The acute Helvetius', cited by Atwood as a witness of transmutation and of the transcendent Light found at the centre; a worthy disciple of Paracelsus.
E0745.body: Atwood names Helvetius with Van Helmont, Crollius, Fludd and Faber as intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus [I.1 ¶64], and cites his explicit transmutation story in support [I.1 ¶77]. His 'Armed Magnet' is identified with the Wheel of Fire or inner Sun [II.3 ¶54]. From his *Vitulus Aureus*, 'the acute Helvetius' is cited as testifying to the transcendent Light and to finding the mystery, by experience, at the centre: “that most recreant Beauty can never be blotted out from my mind” [III.1 ¶70; III.1 n74]; how far the cited words are his own is not clear from the passage.

E0746.summary: Philosopher Atwood cites repeatedly in support: the dry soul, living the death of others, the principle named fire, and the Well where Truth lies hidden.
E0746.body: Atwood says Heraclitus' metaphysics agrees in essentials with Aristotle's [I.1 ¶16], and cites him as supporting that the theurgic media are medicines of imperfect souls [II.2 ¶5]. For the dry, self-turned soul she quotes “a dry soul is the wisest” [II.3 ¶27]; for nox corporis, souls dead to this life and alive in the other, “we live their death and die their life” [II.4 ¶9]. He is cited as naming the principle, according to essence, fire: “have denominated it to be fire” [III.2 ¶35]. The Wisdom is 'that Well of Heraclitus' where Truth lies hidden, 'whence also those philosophic tears' [IV.4 ¶27]. Atwood uses him in support or illustration throughout.

E0747.summary: Figure whose cleansing of the Augean Stable figures, in the Appendix, the cleansing of the mineral soul.
E0747.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Hercules' labour of cleansing the Augean Stable figures the cleansing of the mineral soul [APP ¶71], and his grief for Hylas illustrates the same point as the Iliad [APP ¶109]. In the main text, Hippocrates is said to have been honored by the Athenians with the same gifts as Hercules and Aesculapius [IV.3 ¶34].

E0748.summary: Author of De Hermetica Aegyptior, vetere et Paracelsior. Nova Medicina, criticized by Atwood for trying to slight alchemy as a recent invention.
E0748.body: Atwood criticizes Herman Conringius, author of *De Hermetica Aegyptior, vetere et Paracelsior. Nova Medicina.*, for trying to slight alchemy as a recent invention [I.1 ¶3; I.1 n1].

E0749.summary: Author of Probier Stein, listed by Atwood among persecuted adepts.
E0749.body: Herman Fichtuld, cited for his *Probier Stein*, is listed among persecuted adepts [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶70; I.1 n79].

E0750.summary: The adept king credited with the Hermetic writings, whose Golden Treatise Atwood prints and glosses, and a constantly cited authority on the work, its agents and its moral conditions.
E0750.body:
Hermes (Trismegistus) is the starting point of the Hermetic story, an adept king credited with the Hermetic writings [I.1 ¶6; I.1 ¶7]; the works imputed to him were translated from Greek into Latin by Ficinus [I.1 ¶64]. Geber ranks after him, and Artephius learned the art from his books [I.1 ¶31; I.1 ¶36]; Norton's verse lists him among masters who “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15].

**Golden Treatise (Tract. Aur.).** Introduced as an ancient epitome of the whole Art of doubtful authorship [I.2 ¶50], it is printed in full as the main text of I.3 and glossed in Atwood's notes [I.3 ¶1–¶58]; she calls it a fair, less sophistical example of alchemical writing, yet veiled [I.3 ¶46]. Its key lines: “the work is both with you and about you” [I.3 ¶1]; “the masculine truly is the heaven of the feminine, and the feminine is the earth of the masculine” [I.3 ¶15]; “the whole matter I know to be one only thing” [I.3 ¶36]; “that which is born of the crow is the beginning of this Art” [I.3 ¶46]. 'Hermes the King' first declared that Mercury cannot be mortified alone [I.3 n17]. Atwood reinterprets its Water as the ethereal body, not common water [I.2 ¶43; I.2 n41], and cites it throughout: the vessel is the water, “vas philosophorum est aqua eorum” [II.1 ¶8]; “Extract from the ray its shadow and its obscurity” [II.3 ¶27]; two natures mortified together [III.1 ¶43]; “Take, my son, the flying bird and drown it flying” [III.1 ¶53; IV.1 ¶15], where she notes he 'does not speak of it openly' [III.1 n67]; the chain binding the matter [III.2 ¶22]; secrecy toward the vicious [III.4 ¶9]; the science as “the sole gift of the living God” [III.4 ¶20].

**Other works.** The separation precept (cited with the Tract. Aur., the Smaragdine Tablet and the Asclepius), “Thou shalt separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross”, is read as Mind the Separator [III.1 ¶21; III.1 n22]; the Tablet is quoted in full as summary instruction, “That which is above is as that which is below” [IV.2 ¶43]. The Poemander (Pymander) testifies to inward regeneration: “For this Mind in men is God” [II.1 ¶43]; “Conceive well the Light in thy Mind, and Know It.” [III.3 ¶52]; each principle carries “the seed of his own regeneration” [IV.2 ¶18]. Knowledge of the First Cause is “a most Divine Silence, and a rest of all the senses” [IV.2 ¶33].

**Practice (IV.3).** He supports the First Key and beheading the Raven [IV.3 ¶3], the Stone as “the vine of the Wise” [IV.3 ¶5], keeping the earthy residue [IV.3 ¶7], “The first of all is the water which issueth out of this Stone.” [IV.3 ¶8], and the permanent union of purified bodies and spirits [IV.3 ¶10]. He names the Spirit of Universal nature “a Quintessence” [III.2 ¶36]. Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): the Poemander on the downward-born nature [APP ¶18]; the Golden Treatise cap. 4 [APP ¶51].

**Also cited.** Trismegistus as acquainted with the divine water [I.1 ¶20]; the Stone generated with light and bringing forth clouds and darkness [II.3 ¶30]; furnace and glass making a new world, via Fludd's Mosaica [II.3 ¶52; II.3 n58]; “our Son, as Hermes calls him”, a personification of the intellectual purpose [III.1 ¶36]; equal Spirits, “both need the help of the other” [III.1 ¶41]; the necessity of labor, via Eirenaeus [IV.1 ¶6], and his toil for 'the blessed Lunary of Diana' [III.2 ¶64]; in Norton's verse, the water of crude Mercury [III.3 ¶74] and “Ignis et Azoth tibi sufficient” [IV.2 ¶13].

E0751.summary: Apparently a name for the Matter, whose many epithets (heaven, water, mercury, salt nitre, sulfur, caput mortuum and others) are said to be those of Hermes' Bird, never at rest.
E0751.body: In a passage voiced by Synesius and the New Light, a list of names for the Matter (heaven, water, mercury, salt nitre, sulfur, caput mortuum and others) closes: “And these are the Epithetes of Hermes, his Bird, which is never at rest.” [I.2 ¶33]. The Bird thus apparently stands for the Matter itself.

E0752.summary: In the Marrow of Alchemy, the closure of the single glass holding the composition.
E0752.body: In verse quoted from the *Marrow of Alchemy*, the single glass holding the composition is closed “which shut With Hermes’ seal, no fear it should be lost” [IV.3 ¶23]. The text does not explain the seal further.

E0753.summary: Ancient fragments whose 'soul-stirring syllables', Atwood says, agree in the same divine tradition.
E0753.body: Atwood cites the Hermetic and Chaldaic Fragments in support: their 'soul-stirring syllables' agree in the same divine tradition [IV.4 ¶28].

E0754.summary: The art at the centre of the book: the perfecting of the mineral life in man, an operation on the Undetermined Subject, identified with Theurgy and with Alchemy.
E0754.body:
Atwood defines the Art as the perfecting of the mineral life in man, typifying the celestial and Divine: “The Art is a question put to Nature respecting the first cause” [APP ¶48] (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer). In the main text it is the right disposition and manipulation of the Undetermined Subject through stated operations; riches come to “he that knows the Art, and the expressions, and hath the medium” [II.2 ¶18]. By it the Matter, having “worked out its own restitution”, is brought into the fixity of its Final Cause [III.2 ¶22]. A passage of uncertain voice makes Art complete what nature cannot, adding supernatural light by graduation, and “leaves the victory to Art” [II.1 ¶25]; in Vaughan it unites a Particular Spirit to the Universal [II.1 ¶25].

History: Democritus' Sacred Physics “treats especially of the Hermetic art, and that occult discovery on which the systems of ancient philosophy appear to have been very uniformly based” [I.1 ¶12]; Bacon stated “the roots of the Hermetic science” while concealing practice [I.1 ¶39]; Flamel's name is honorably connected with it [I.1 ¶56]; Atwood distinguishes “the genuine Hermetic art” from pretenders' follies [I.1 ¶64]. Its ground is “as far out of the road of common thought as if it were tabooed” [I.1 ¶76]. It is cabalistic and veiled, plain in itself but in metaphor: “For is not our art cabalistic” [I.1 ¶84]; the world is ignorant of “the genuine doctrine and Art of Wisdom” [I.1 ¶86].

Identities: = Theurgy and = Art of Divine works: “Now the Egyptians, that is the Hermetic Art, or Art of Divine works, was by the Greeks called Theurgy” [II.2 ¶3], practised in the Mysteries [II.2 ¶2]; = Alchemy, “the most commendable art of Alchemy” [I.1 ¶84]. Labels such as 'the Secret Art', 'the Divine Art' and 'the Great Art' also occur near I.1 ¶39–¶43, but no explicit identity among them is asserted there.

E0755.summary: The Art whose province is to resuscitate the buried Source of reason and bring it, through self-knowledge, into living experience.
E0755.body: Atwood: “this it is the province of Hermetic Artifice to resuscitate and bring through self-knowledge into the experience of life” [IV.4 ¶20], the thing resuscitated being the buried Source of reason.

E0756.summary: The operation that obtains the right recipient, separates pure from impure and subtle from gross, and makes agent and patient one.
E0756.body: Atwood: “by the Hermetic dissolution the right recipient is said to be obtained” [I.2 ¶48]; the same operation separates pure from impure and subtle from gross, and makes agent and patient one [I.2 ¶48].

E0757.summary: The theory of the art as acquired by reading, which requires the same faculties as the later experimental proof.
E0757.body: Atwood says the same faculties are needed “in acquiring the Hermetic doctrine, by perusal, as is afterwards needed for the experimental proof” [III.4 ¶15].

E0758.summary: The practical work itself, whose method and true basis Atwood says the passages she has gathered clarify.
E0758.body: Atwood presents her cited passages as clarifying matters “with respect to the method and true basis of the Hermetic experiment” [III.1 ¶71].

E0759.summary: The means by which ancient fables were interpreted as philosophy.
E0759.body: Atwood mentions writers who “explained them by the Hermetic key” [I.1 ¶70], i.e. read ancient fable as philosophy; the passage does not say what the key is.

E0760.summary: The agent and patient aspects of the one self-purifying subject; in full advancement, the Sun and Moon philosophical.
E0760.body: Atwood: the one self-purifying subject is “in turn agent and patient, which are the Hermetic luminaries; in their full representative advancement, the Sun and Moon philosophical” [II.2 ¶26]. Asserted identities: = agent and patient; = Sun and Moon philosophical [II.2 ¶26].

E0761.summary: The voice Atwood cites from the Tract. Aur., cited on the crowned operator, the moral qualifications for Wisdom, and Wisdom as a gift.
E0761.body: Quoting the Tract. Aur. (and Ripley Revived), Atwood cites the Hermetic Master on the accomplished operator: “henceforth thou art a Crowned King, resting over the Fountain” [III.3 ¶17; III.3 n9]; on the moral qualifications for entry into hidden Wisdom, one must strive “to free himself from the usurpation of vice, and to be good, just, and of sound reason” [III.4 ¶15; III.4 n10]; and on Wisdom as not won by effort: “Wisdom was with thee, says the Hermetic Master; it was not gotten by thy care” [IV.1 ¶40; IV.1 n31]. All are cited in support.

E0762.summary: The work and its end, figured as a line that returns into its beginning to form a circle, joined in Eternity rather than in time.
E0762.body: Atwood: “This is the work --- this is the Hermetic method and its end” [IV.3 ¶62], figured as “The line returns to form a circle into its’ beginning, and they join not in time, for their union is Eternity.” [IV.3 ¶62]. Asserted identity: = the work [IV.3 ¶62].

E0763.summary: The subject of the whole book: a genuine tradition whose nucleus is Life and whose Key is Light, culminating in divine illumination.
E0763.body: Atwood defends “the genuine tradition of Hermetic science” against sophists' deceits, holding that public disbelief “are no proofs in philosophy, even if it were without so many witnesses, that the Hermetic mystery is groundless” [I.1 ¶86]. After describing the divine illumination she writes “That was the sum of the Hermetic Mystery” [IV.2 ¶43], the sum being also the ultimate object of the Alchemical Art; what 'that' covers is apparently most directly the illumination of IV.2 ¶39–¶42, but its exact extent is not certain. Finally: “And Life is the nucleus of the whole Hermetic Mystery, and the Key thereof is Light” [IV.4 ¶32].

E0764.summary: Practitioners of the Hermetic art; a title Atwood withholds from Aristotle and Plato without further evidence that they practised it.
E0764.body: Atwood will not grant Aristotle or Plato the title without more evidence that they practised the art, evidence needed “to prove their claim to the title of Hermetic philosophers” [I.1 ¶17]. Practitioners of the Hermetic art are so called [I.1 ¶12].

E0765.summary: Experimental inquiry into the Universal Spirit through man; universal, rational and divine knowledge beside which worldly science is relatively vain.
E0765.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood calls Hermetic Philosophy experimentation into the Universal Spirit through man, “a development of the art by which a particular spirit (to use Vaughan’s words) is allied to the universal” [APP ¶53]. In the main text it is knowledge described as universal, rational and divine, beside which worldly science is relatively vain, with “the ground of the whole Hermetic philosophy laid out” [I.1 ¶64].

E0766.summary: A regular inquisition into life, in which motion is present with interrogation.
E0766.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The Hermetic Process is a regular inquisition into life.” [APP ¶138]; in it motion is present with interrogation.
